task: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
question: A document-intake pipeline runs two Claude stages on the same model. Stage one routes about 400,000 incoming emails a day into one of six queues, using labels that human reviewers agree on almost without exception. Stage two drafts a monthly regulatory analysis that reasons across dozens of filings. Finance asks the architect to cut cost. Which recommendation is best?

options.A: Move both stages to the smallest model, since a single uniform tier keeps the pipeline simpler to operate
options.B: Keep both stages on the current model, since any model change risks quality regressions in production
options.C: Evaluate a smaller model on the routing stage against a labeled set and switch only if it meets the bar
options.D: Move the regulatory stage to a smaller model, since it runs only monthly and its volume is negligible

rationale: The cost sits in the high-volume routing stage, whose crisp labels make it the stage most likely to be served by a smaller model, and the switch is justified by evaluation rather than assumed. Moving everything down (A) ignores the deep reasoning stage two needs. Refusing any change (B) forgoes a saving the evidence may well support; model changes are managed with evaluation, not avoided. Downsizing the regulatory stage (D) targets the stage with negligible volume and the highest reasoning demand, saving little while risking the most.
evidence: Model selection is a cost-latency-quality tradeoff argued from the task, not brand preference.

task: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
question: A legal team's summarization assistant must cite sources in an in-house citation style with several irregular cases (consolidated dockets, sealed exhibits, superseded rulings). The summaries are accurate, but citations for the irregular cases come out inconsistent, and two rewrites of the prose description of the style have not helped. The team has a set of correctly cited documents. What should the architect change first?

options.A: Fine-tune a model on the firm's past briefs so that the citation style is learned in the weights
options.B: Add worked examples of each irregular case to the prompt, then re-test on held-out documents
options.C: Expand the prose description of the style and mark the irregular-case rules as critical in capitals
options.D: Ask the model to reason step by step about each citation before it writes the final summary

rationale: A format that is hard to state in prose is best conveyed by demonstration: few-shot examples covering exactly the failing irregular cases, checked on documents that were not used as examples. Fine-tuning (A) is the slow, expensive answer to a problem that examples in the prompt already solve. More prose and emphasis (C) repeats the approach that has failed twice. Chain-of-thought (D) helps multi-step reasoning, but the failure is an unfamiliar output format, not a reasoning error, and more reasoning without a reference pattern does not show the model what the style looks like.
evidence: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

task: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
question: An account-research agent calls a CRM lookup tool six to eight times per task. Each call returns the full account record, about 15,000 tokens of history and metadata, although the agent only ever uses the contact name, account tier and renewal date. Long tasks now hit the context limit, and reasoning in the later steps degrades. Which change best addresses the problem?

options.A: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window so that all of the records fit
options.B: Enable prompt caching on the tool results so the repeated records cost less per call
options.C: Instruct the agent in its system prompt to ignore every record field it does not need
options.D: Have the tool return only the fields the task uses before results enter the context

rationale: The context is being spent on data the task never uses; trimming the tool's output at the source keeps each call to a few hundred tokens, which addresses both the limit and the dilution that degrades later reasoning. A larger window (A) delays the same failure at higher cost and leaves the irrelevant material in place. Caching (B) reuses a stable prefix to cut cost and latency, but it does not reduce how much of the window the records occupy. An instruction to ignore fields (C) still sends every token into the context, so neither the limit nor the dilution changes.
evidence: Optimize context windows and manage token usage

task: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
question: Twelve internal assistants each carry their own pasted copy of the same compliance disclaimer and escalation procedure in their system prompts. Legal revised the wording a month ago; four assistants still use the old text, and nobody can say which version each assistant was running last week. What should the architect put in place?

options.A: A single versioned module for the shared block, referenced by every assistant and reviewed on change
options.B: Prompt caching on each assistant's system prompt so the shared disclaimer is processed only once
options.C: A quarterly audit that compares every assistant's copy with legal's master text and fixes differences
options.D: One merged assistant to replace all twelve, so that only a single system prompt is left to maintain

rationale: The failure is duplicated prompt content drifting silently. Factoring the shared block into one versioned module that every assistant references means a change is made once, reviewed, and traceable to a version. Caching (B) is a cost and latency mechanism; it neither propagates new wording nor records which version ran. A quarterly audit (C) is a detective control that leaves assistants out of date for months. Merging the assistants (D) throws away their specialisation to solve a maintenance problem that modular prompts solve directly.
evidence: Prompt reuse at enterprise scale means modular prompts, versioning, and Skills, so behavior changes are reviewable events rather than silent drift.

task: Implement guardrails and safety controls
question: A customer-service assistant looks up orders through a tool that accepts any order number. Its only protection is a system-prompt rule never to disclose other customers' orders. A red-team tester obtained another customer's delivery address by supplying that customer's order number with a plausible story. The product owner proposes rewording the rule more forcefully. What should the architect recommend instead?

options.A: Log every order lookup and have the support team review those logs weekly for suspicious access
options.B: Scope the lookup tool to the authenticated customer's orders and add an output check as a layer
options.C: Keep the reworded rule and move to a larger model that follows system instructions more reliably
options.D: Require customers to restate the order number twice before the assistant reveals any details

rationale: The prompt rule is a single layer, and it has already failed. Restricting the tool to the authenticated customer's own orders removes the capability that was abused, and an output check adds an independent layer behind it. Weekly log review (A) detects a leak after the data is gone. A stronger rule on a larger model (C) is still one bypassable prompt-level layer. Restating the number (D) does nothing against an attacker who already has it.
evidence: Layer guardrails: input validation, output filtering, scoped permissions, human-in-the-loop for consequential actions. One layer is a single point of failure.

task: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
question: A recruiting firm will use Claude to shortlist applicants for interview. Validated against recruiters' past decisions, the shortlister agrees 94% of the time overall, and the team has already removed names and photos from its inputs. Applicants are not currently told how shortlists are produced. Before launch, the ethics review asks for one more addition. Which is most important?

options.A: Senior recruiters reviewing a random sample of shortlists every week and correcting any poor picks
options.B: Also redacting universities and postcodes, since those fields can act as proxies for background
options.C: Raising agreement with recruiters' past decisions to 98% on a larger and more recent validation set
options.D: Comparing shortlist rates between applicant groups, and disclosing the model's role to candidates

rationale: Nothing yet measures whether outcomes differ between groups: a 94% aggregate can hide large gaps, and agreement with past recruiter decisions can simply reproduce their bias. Applicants are also unaware that a model is involved. Comparing outcomes across groups and disclosing the model's role closes both gaps. Weekly recruiter sampling (A) judges shortlists against the same recruiter standard that may carry the bias, and a random sample does not compare groups. Redacting more fields (B) is a sensible mitigation, but like the first redaction it is unmeasured, so nobody can tell whether a disparity remains. A higher agreement target (C) is still an aggregate tied to past decisions, so closer agreement can mean closer reproduction of past bias.
evidence: Ethics is scored concretely: bias testing, fairness across user groups, transparency about AI involvement.

task: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
question: A US federal agency plans a cloud-hosted Claude assistant to help its caseworkers answer benefit inquiries. Some inquiries include applicants' medical details, and a small share come from applicants living in the EU. The agency CIO asks which regulatory consideration decides which hosting environments the solution may use at all. Which answer is best?

options.A: HIPAA, since medical details in the inquiries must be de-identified before they leave the agency
options.B: GDPR, since applicants in the EU mean the service has to be hosted in an EU region to serve them
options.C: FedRAMP, since a federal agency may only deploy to cloud services authorized for federal use
options.D: The agency's records-retention schedule, since every transcript must be kept for a set period

rationale: The question is which environments the agency may deploy to at all, and for a US federal agency's cloud deployment that is what FedRAMP governs: authorized environments carrying the required controls. HIPAA (A) is relevant to how health information flows through the design, but it is a data-handling obligation, not the rule that determines which cloud environments a federal agency may use. GDPR (B) is about how personal data of people in the EU is processed (minimization, purpose limitation, erasure) and touches only a small share of inquiries; it does not decide the agency's hosting environment. A retention schedule (D) shapes what is stored and for how long, not where the solution may run.
evidence: US federal cloud deployments: authorized environments and controls

task: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
question: At kickoff, an insurer's COO says, "We want a Claude agent for claims." The engineering team, keen to show momentum, proposes building a multi-agent prototype over the next two weeks. Nobody has yet said which part of claims handling is costly, what constraints apply, or how success would be measured. What should the architect do first?

options.A: Run structured discovery on the problem, constraints and success measures before choosing a design
options.B: Build the prototype quickly, since a working demo is the fastest way to surface the real requirements
options.C: Choose the model and orchestration framework first, since those choices constrain every later decision
options.D: Request all historical claims data so the team can explore it and find where an agent would add value

rationale: With no stated problem, constraints or success measure, any design, including the choice of an agent at all, is a guess. Discovery comes before architecture. A prototype (B) commits to a multi-agent design before anyone knows whether the problem needs one, and its demo cannot be judged without success measures. Picking the model and framework (C) is a design decision taken before the requirement exists. A bulk data request (D) is exploration without a question, and it raises data-handling obligations before any purpose has been established.
evidence: Structured discovery before design: business problem, constraints, success measures, then architecture.

task: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
question: Three months after launch, business users of a contract-review assistant keep reporting that it is "too slow". Requests range from quick clause lookups to full reviews of 80-page agreements, and no response-time target was ever agreed for either. The team has made several tuning changes, and after each one the complaints continue. What should the architect do next?

options.A: Move full reviews to a faster model once an evaluation confirms that review quality is maintained
options.B: Enable streaming so text appears sooner, then survey users after a month on whether it feels faster
options.C: Add per-request latency dashboards so the team can see exactly where the time is being spent
options.D: Agree with the business how fast each kind of request must be, then track and report against that

rationale: The complaints persist because nobody has defined fast enough for either kind of request, so no change can be shown to have succeeded. Agreeing a target per request type with the business, then measuring and reporting against it, turns the complaint into a shared, testable expectation. A faster model (A) is a reasonable lever, but without a target nobody knows whether the result will be fast enough or whether the lookups were the problem. Streaming plus a survey (B) improves perceived speed and gathers opinions, but it still leaves no agreed threshold to judge against. Dashboards (C) show where time goes inside the team, but they do not tell the team what speed the business expects.
evidence: expectations get managed with explicit SLAs

task: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
question: A Claude solution was handed over to a client's platform team, which now owns it and must evolve it independently. The handoff package was a complete set of architecture diagrams. Within a month the team moved a per-user greeting to the top of the system prompt, which broke prompt caching and raised costs, and removed a validation step they believed was redundant. Neither change contradicted the diagrams. What should future handoffs add?

options.A: Diagrams annotated with every prompt section and pipeline step, kept current in the client's wiki
options.B: A written account of why each design choice was made and the constraints any change must respect
options.C: A hands-on session walking the client team through how to operate and deploy each component
options.D: A sign-off step in which the architect's team reviews every prompt or pipeline edit before release

rationale: Both changes were reasonable-looking edits that broke an unstated constraint: static content goes first so caching works, and the validation step is a guardrail. What the client lacked was the reasoning behind the design, so handoff must carry the reasons and the constraints that later changes have to respect. Annotated diagrams (A) record more of what was built, but the edits did not contradict the diagrams, so more detail on structure would not have prevented them. An operations walkthrough (C) teaches how to run and deploy the system, not why it is built the way it is. Architect sign-off (D) catches errors only by keeping the original team in the loop, which contradicts the requirement that the client evolve the solution independently.
evidence: handoff includes implementation guidance, not just diagrams

task: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
question: A platform team connects one internal agent to five MCP servers (CRM, billing, HR, ticketing, wiki) that together expose 140 tools. The definitions take about 45,000 tokens of every request before the user says a word, and logs show the agent calls a similarly named tool from the wrong system in roughly one call in eight. Most conversations touch only two of the five systems. Which change best addresses both the token cost and the wrong-tool calls?

options.A: Defer most tools behind a tool-search step and keep only the handful used most often loaded in context.
options.B: Move to a model with a larger context window, so the full tool list no longer crowds out the conversation.
options.C: Enable prompt caching on the tool definitions, so the 45,000 tokens are billed at the lower cached rate.
options.D: Rewrite every tool description to be as short as possible, so the 140 definitions take far fewer tokens.

rationale: Tool search with deferred loading keeps only a few frequently used tools in context and pulls in others when the agent searches for them, so the 140-tool catalog neither costs 45,000 tokens per request nor competes during selection. Shorter descriptions (D) save tokens but remove the detail that separates look-alike tools, which worsens wrong-tool calls. Caching (C) lowers the price of the same tokens but leaves all 140 candidates in front of the model. A larger window (B) fixes neither the cost nor the confusion between similar tools.
evidence: Tool search suits large or growing toolsets where definitions are heavy and selection accuracy drops; deferred tools load only when discovered, and a few frequent tools stay loaded.

task: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
question: A finance team builds an agent that answers questions about last quarter's revenue through an MCP server wrapping the company's Postgres warehouse. The server connects with the database owner's credentials and exposes run_sql, insert_rows and drop_table tools. Security requires least privilege that does not depend on the model behaving, enforced both where the database authenticates the server and in what the agent can request. Which TWO changes meet this? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Remove insert_rows and drop_table from the toolset the agent receives, so write operations cannot even be requested.
options.B: Connect the server through a dedicated database role that holds SELECT only on the revenue schemas the agent needs.
options.C: Add a rule to the system prompt telling the agent to run only SELECT statements and never to modify any data.
options.D: Wrap run_sql in a filter that rejects any statement containing the keywords DROP, DELETE or UPDATE before it executes.
options.E: Log every statement the agent runs and page the security team whenever a statement modifies data in the warehouse.

rationale: Least privilege has to hold even if the model misbehaves, so it is enforced at two layers: a read-only database role (B) means no statement can write whatever is sent, and removing the write tools (A) keeps the capability out of the agent's configuration entirely. A prompt rule (C) is probabilistic, logging and paging (E) detect misuse only after the data has changed, and a keyword filter (D) is easy to evade with statements it does not anticipate while the owner credential remains behind it.
evidence: Least privilege removes capabilities and credentials a role does not need; prompts and after-the-fact logging are not substitutes for enforced scopes.

task: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
question:
An HR assistant reaches the payroll API through a remote MCP server. After an employee complaint, auditors extract this log and the policy that applies.

```text
09:14:02 user=maria.k tool=get_payslip employee=e-3381 downstream_principal=svc-hr-agent status=200
09:14:40 user=tom.w   tool=get_payslip employee=e-1029 downstream_principal=svc-hr-agent status=200
09:15:11 user=tom.w   tool=get_payslip employee=e-0017 downstream_principal=svc-hr-agent status=200
policy: employees read only their own payslip; managers read their direct reports'
```

Tom is not a manager. Which gap does the log show, and what fixes it?

options.A: The payroll API sees only a shared service identity, so it cannot apply per-user rules; exchange the user's token for a downstream token that carries that user's identity.
options.B: The service credential lives too long; shorten its lifetime and rotate it every hour so a stolen token loses value quickly.
options.C: The model is choosing employee ids that do not belong to the caller; add few-shot examples that show each user's own id being used in the call.
options.D: The payroll API has no request throttling; add a per-user quota in the MCP server so one user cannot read many payslips.

rationale: Every call reaches payroll as svc-hr-agent, so the API cannot tell Tom from a manager and has no per-user decision to make; the server must obtain a downstream token that represents the signed-in user so the API's own authorization applies (not a raw passthrough of a token issued for another audience). Examples (C) try to fix an authorization gap with model behavior. Rotating the credential (B) is hygiene that leaves the shared identity in place. A quota (D) slows reads but still allows reading other people's payslips.
evidence: MCP servers must not pass through tokens not issued to them; downstream access should carry proper user-bound credentials so resource servers can enforce their own authorization.

task: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
question: A law firm's research assistant retrieves from one shared vector index that holds documents from every client matter. Each chunk carries an access list that is synced from the document management system once a night. An associate was shown a passage from Matter B, from which she had been removed that afternoon. The system prompt already says to answer only from the user's own matters. Which TWO changes close the gap? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Pass the verified identity from the authenticated session to the retriever and filter candidate chunks by matter access before ranking.
options.B: Add a post-generation check that deletes any sentence that appears to come from a matter the user is not assigned to.
options.C: Refresh the access lists whenever the document management system emits a permission change, instead of waiting for the nightly sync.
options.D: Encrypt the vector index at rest and in transit so that passages from other matters cannot be read by outsiders.
options.E: Reword the system prompt more forcefully so the model refuses to quote any matter the user is not assigned to.

rationale: Two separate failures are visible: the filter is not enforced where data is retrieved, and the permission data it would use is up to a day stale. Filtering on the authenticated user's access before ranking (A) means unauthorized text never reaches the model, and event-driven permission updates (C) make a same-day revocation take effect. Prompt wording (E) and a post-hoc sentence check (B) leave the text in the model's context and rely on probabilistic behavior. Encryption (D) protects against outsiders, not against an authorized system returning the wrong rows.
evidence: Enforce authorization in the data path with the caller's verified identity, not by instructing the model; the system must also reflect permission changes promptly.

task: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
question:
A company indexes 4,000 supplier contracts as fixed 400-token chunks whose only metadata is an opaque file id and chunk number. A user asks, "What is the liability cap in the Halvorsen supply agreement?" The top results are below, and the engineer cannot tell which, if any, belongs to Halvorsen.

```text
query: liability cap Halvorsen supply agreement
1. 0.81  "...aggregate liability shall not exceed the fees paid in the preceding twelve months."  [c-0412 #37]
2. 0.79  "...liability shall not exceed two times the annual contract value, excluding indemnities."  [c-2291 #12]
3. 0.77  "...neither party shall be liable for indirect or consequential damages arising from..."  [c-0873 #40]
```

Which change to the pipeline best fixes this failure?

options.A: Prepend a description of the contract and section, naming the parties, to each chunk before embedding and keyword indexing.
options.B: Re-embed every chunk with a higher-dimensional embedding model to separate near-identical liability clauses.
options.C: Add a reranker that rescores the retrieved chunks against the query text before they are passed to the model.
options.D: Raise the number of retrieved chunks from 3 to 30 and let the model work out which of the clauses belongs to the Halvorsen agreement.

rationale: The chunks are the right kind of clause, but nothing in their text says whose contract they are, so neither semantic nor keyword matching can single out Halvorsen. Adding chunk-specific context (parties, agreement type, section) before embedding and BM25 indexing puts the missing identity into the searchable text. More chunks (D) just adds more anonymous clauses. A reranker (C) scores the same context-free text, and a larger embedding (B) cannot encode a name that is absent from the chunk.
evidence: Contextual retrieval prepends chunk-specific explanatory context before embedding and BM25 indexing, because isolated chunks often lack the subject they refer to.

task: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
question:
A maintenance assistant for industrial pumps retrieves service bulletins with dense embeddings only. Technicians often search by exact fault or part codes. Here is a trace of three queries.

```text
q1 "why does the pump trip on fault code F-2217?" -> rank 1 SB-118 (documents F-2217)
q2 "F-2217"                                         -> rank 1 SB-044 (F-2271), rank 2 SB-203 (F-2127), SB-118 at rank 9
q3 "torque spec part 77-3109-B"                     -> rank 1 SB-310 (77-3190-B), SB-250 (77-3109-B) at rank 6
```

Which change best fits this failure pattern?

options.A: Add lexical (BM25) retrieval alongside the embeddings and merge the two rankings, so exact identifiers match exactly.
options.B: Increase chunk size to 1,500 tokens so that each bulletin's surrounding explanation is available when a code is matched.
options.C: Fine-tune the embedding model on past technician queries so that it learns the company's fault codes as vocabulary.
options.D: Have Claude rewrite short queries into full natural-language questions before they are embedded and searched.

rationale: The long natural-language query works, but bare identifiers return near-miss codes (F-2271, 77-3190-B), the classic weakness of dense retrieval on exact tokens. Lexical retrieval matches the string itself, and fusing it with embeddings keeps semantic recall for the descriptive queries. Fine-tuning (C) is heavy and still maps codes into fuzzy vector space. Bigger chunks (B) do not change how the codes are matched. Query rewriting (D) helps phrasing, but a rewritten query still goes to the same embedding comparison that confuses similar codes.
evidence: Embeddings capture semantic similarity while BM25 matches precise terms such as unique identifiers; combining them handles both kinds of query.

task: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
question: A retailer wants an assistant that answers questions such as "What was the return rate for footwear in the Midwest in Q3 compared with Q2?" The data sits in a 40-million-row sales table. The prototype splits CSV exports into chunks, embeds them and retrieves the top 10; answers read fluently but the numbers are wrong. What should the architect change?

options.A: Split the CSV exports into larger chunks that each hold a full region-quarter of rows, then retrieve the top 10 of those.
options.B: Pre-write a narrative summary of every month's sales and embed those summaries instead of the raw rows.
options.C: Increase the retrieval depth from 10 to 200 chunks, so that many more of the relevant rows reach the model.
options.D: Give the agent a read-only SQL query tool over the warehouse, so the database computes the aggregates.

rationale: The question is an aggregation over a large structured table, and no top-k set of text chunks can contain every row needed; a query tool lets the database compute the exact figure and Claude explain it. Retrieving 200 chunks (C) is still a sample of 40 million rows, bigger chunks (A) hold more rows yet remain partial, and pre-written summaries (B) cover only the slices someone anticipated and cannot answer an arbitrary region-quarter comparison.
evidence: Retrieval must match the data shape and query pattern; structured, aggregate questions call for structured query tools rather than similarity search over text chunks.

task: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
question: An operations team keeps 220 incident runbooks, roughly 3 million tokens in total. Each incident needs two or three of them, which ones depends on triage, and the steps must be followed exactly as written, including exact commands. Incidents often span several owning teams. Which context strategy fits best?

options.A: Embed 300-token runbook chunks and inject the five chunks most similar to the alert into the prompt for each alert.
options.B: Compress all 220 runbooks into one digest of their key steps and keep that digest in the prompt for every single incident.
options.C: Load each team's full runbook set into a cached prompt chosen by the alert's source.
options.D: Keep a short catalog of titles and use-when lines in context, and let the agent open the runbook it needs.

rationale: A compact catalog is always in context and the agent reads only the complete runbooks that triage points to, so exact commands arrive intact and the context stays small however many runbooks exist. A digest (B) loses the exact steps. Five similar chunks (A) can split a procedure and miss steps that don't resemble the alert. Team-based cached sets (C) still load hundreds of thousands of irrelevant tokens and fail when an incident spans teams.
evidence: Progressive disclosure loads lightweight metadata first and the full instructions or resources only when needed, keeping context small.

task: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
question: A pharmacy-benefits company's coverage assistant answers questions from one formulary document of about 90,000 tokens that is revised each quarter. Traffic is steady at 40 requests a minute. Nearly every question needs several sections cross-referenced (tiers, step therapy, exclusions) and the answer must cite section numbers. An engineer proposes a vector index with 512-token chunks. Which design is best?

options.A: Send the formulary uncached, since it changes only quarterly and caching adds a write premium.
options.B: Index 512-token chunks and retrieve the top eight of them, because retrieval keeps each request's input small and cheap.
options.C: Summarize each section of the document and retrieve the summaries, so the model sees an outline of every part.
options.D: Place the whole formulary first in a cached prefix with the question after it, and refresh the cache at each revision.

rationale: A stable 90,000-token document that nearly every request needs fits comfortably in context, and a cached prefix makes the repeated read fast and cheap at steady traffic while keeping all sections visible for cross-references and citations. Top-eight chunks (B) can miss the second or third section a question depends on. Section summaries (C) lose the exact wording needed for citations. Sending it uncached (A) throws away the saving: with 40 requests a minute the prefix is read back at the cached rate long before the 5-minute TTL expires.
evidence: If a knowledge base is small enough, include it in the prompt; prompt caching makes this faster and cheaper than building a retrieval pipeline.

task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
question: An insurer's engineering group wants its internal claims-lookup service used by three different clients: Claude Code for developers, a desktop assistant for adjusters, and a custom agent that a partner team is building. Each team currently plans to write its own tool wrapper around the service's REST API. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Expose the claims service as an agent that the three clients delegate to over an agent-to-agent protocol.
options.B: Ship a command-line client for the service and have all three clients call it through a shell tool.
options.C: Publish an OpenAPI description of the REST API and let each team generate its own wrapper from it.
options.D: Build one MCP server in front of the claims service, with the access control the service requires, and connect all three clients to it.

rationale: A single MCP server is the standard, reusable connector: it defines the tools once, with authentication and authorization, and any MCP-capable client can use it. Generated wrappers (C) still leave three separately maintained tool definitions. A CLI (B) assumes every client has a shell, which an adjuster-facing desktop assistant may not. An agent-to-agent interface (A) fits autonomous, multi-turn peers; a lookup service is a tool, not an agent.
evidence: MCP is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems, so one server can serve many clients.

task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
question: A logistics company's dispatch agent must hand delayed-shipment cases to a carrier's own claims agent, built by another vendor on a different framework. The exchange runs over several turns across hours (documents requested, a settlement negotiated), and neither company will expose its internal tools, prompts or data stores to the other. Which integration mechanism fits?

options.A: An agent-to-agent interface in which each side advertises capabilities and exchanges tasks and messages.
options.B: A shared database that both agents write case updates to, polling it for the other side's replies and documents.
options.C: Run the carrier's agent as a subagent inside the dispatch company's orchestrator, using the carrier's prompts and tool code.
options.D: An MCP server run by the carrier that exposes its internal claims tools and data lookups directly to the dispatch agent.

rationale: Two independently owned, opaque agents that negotiate over long-running, multi-turn tasks need a peer interface: a capability description plus task and message exchange across a trust boundary, with each side keeping its internals private. Exposing the carrier's internal tools through MCP (D) breaks that opacity and makes the dispatch agent do the carrier's work. Hosting the carrier's agent as a subagent (C) needs its prompts and code. A polled shared database (B) offers no task semantics, authentication per agent, or negotiation protocol.
evidence: MCP connects an agent to tools and data; peer agents owned by different parties collaborate through agent-to-agent task exchange without exposing internals.

task: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
question: A retail bank's Claude assistant handles 3 million conversations a month, and each turn may call up to six tools. Compliance forbids keeping raw customer text beyond 30 days, and the platform team cannot afford to store every full transcript for debugging. Last month a tool-schema change caused silently wrong answers for two days before anyone noticed. Which monitoring strategy fits?

options.A: Have a reviewer read 20 randomly chosen conversations each week and report any quality problems found there.
options.B: Store every full transcript for 30 days and search those transcripts when customers complain about wrong answers.
options.C: Alert on API error rates and on the provider's status page, since a tool-schema change would surface as visible API failures.
options.D: Record structured metrics and traces for all traffic, and keep full redacted payloads only for sampled or flagged requests.

rationale: At this scale the signal has to be cheap and always on: structured metrics and spans (tokens, latency, stop reason, tool errors by tool version) catch a silent regression within hours, while full payloads, redacted and kept only for a sample and for flagged requests such as errors or low scores, support diagnosis within the retention limit. Storing everything (B) is costly and reactive. A weekly sample of 20 (A) is far too thin to see a two-day regression. API error rates and the status page (C) miss wrong answers that return HTTP 200.
evidence: Production agents need full tracing and metrics to diagnose non-deterministic failures, without necessarily monitoring conversation contents.

task: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
question: A claims-triage system uses a coordinator agent that delegates to four subagents, each calling internal tools. Each component logs to its own file with its own timestamp format, and engineers spend hours piecing together the log lines for a single user request. Last week's quality regression coincided with both a prompt change and a tool-version bump, and the team could not tell which was responsible. Which TWO changes address these two problems? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Ask each subagent to append a self-assessed confidence score to its output and alert whenever that score is low.
options.B: Propagate one trace id from the coordinator through every subagent and tool call so all spans of a request can be joined.
options.C: Copy all component log files onto one shared volume so that engineers can search all of them from a single place.
options.D: Tag each span and metric with the prompt version, model id and tool version, so a regression can be attributed.
options.E: Raise log verbosity to DEBUG on every component so that much more of each request is captured in the log files.

rationale: The first problem is correlation, solved by one trace id carried across agents and tools (B); the second is attribution, solved by stamping version metadata on telemetry so a change in behavior lines up with the prompt, model or tool that changed (D). More verbose logs (E) and a shared volume (C) add volume and a common location but still no join key or version dimension. Self-reported confidence (A) is an unvalidated model signal, not infrastructure telemetry.
evidence: Tracing across agent and tool calls plus structured production telemetry is what lets teams diagnose failures in multi-agent systems.

task: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
question:
A bank's contact-center copilot shows suggested replies while the customer is still speaking. Requirements: accuracy of at least 90% on the golden set and an end-to-end p95 of 2.0 seconds or less. The table shows model time only; retrieval and network add about 0.5 seconds to every request.

```text
config                    accuracy   model p95   cost / 1K calls
Haiku 5.5, effort low       84%        0.7 s        $1.10
Haiku 5.5, effort high      92%        1.7 s        $1.60
Sonnet 5.5, effort low      93%        1.4 s        $3.40
Sonnet 5.5, effort high     96%        4.8 s        $9.80
```

Which configuration should the architect choose?

options.A: Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, because a regulated bank should favor accuracy over response time.
options.B: Haiku 5.5 at high effort, because it is the cheapest configuration that reaches the accuracy requirement.
options.C: Sonnet 5.5 at low effort, which meets both thresholds once the 0.5 seconds of overhead is added.
options.D: Haiku 5.5 at low effort, since it is fastest and prompt work should be able to close the accuracy gap.

rationale: Adding the 0.5 s overhead gives end-to-end p95 of 2.2 s for Haiku at high effort (B), which fails the 2.0 s budget even though it looks cheapest, and 5.3 s for Sonnet at high effort (A). Sonnet at low effort reaches 1.9 s with 93% accuracy, the only configuration meeting both thresholds. Haiku at low effort (D) is fast but 6 points under the bar, and hoping prompt work closes the gap is not a measured result.
evidence: Choose the configuration that meets measured accuracy and latency requirements, counting total request latency, not model time alone.

task: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
question: A travel assistant takes about 6.5 seconds before the customer sees any reply. A trace shows: intent classification 0.4 s; then flight search (1.1 s), hotel search (1.3 s) and loyalty-balance lookup (0.7 s) executed one after another although none depends on another; then a 350-token answer generated in 2.6 s and displayed only when complete. Product will not accept lower answer quality. Which TWO changes cut latency without reducing accuracy? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Stream the answer to the user as it is generated, so the first words appear well before generation finishes.
options.B: Run the three independent lookups concurrently, as parallel tool calls, so they take as long as the slowest one.
options.C: Switch the answer step to the smallest available model without evaluating the change on the golden set.
options.D: Cache each final answer for 24 hours keyed on the query text, since many customers ask similar questions.
options.E: Set max_tokens to 150 so that every answer finishes in roughly half the time it takes now.

rationale: The trace shows two removable delays: 3.1 s of sequential independent lookups, which run in about 1.3 s in parallel (B), and 2.6 s of waiting for a complete answer, which streaming turns into a quick first token (A). A smaller model with no evaluation (C) risks accuracy that product will not accept. A 150-token cap (E) truncates answers and returns stop_reason max_tokens. Caching answers by query text (D) would serve stale fares and availability.
evidence: Independent tool calls can run in parallel, and streaming improves perceived latency though it does not change cost.

task: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
question: A claims platform runs three Claude tasks. (1) Classify 2 million inbound messages a day into 12 intents; an eval shows the smallest tier matching expert labels. (2) Summarize adjuster notes for about 5,000 files a day. (3) Review 300 complex liability disputes a month: after three prompt revisions the mid tier agrees with senior counsel 78% of the time against a required 90%, while the top tier reaches 92% on the same set. Finance wants the lowest cost that still meets each task's quality bar. Which assignment is best?

options.A: Use the smallest tier for the classifier and the top tier for the disputes, and pick the summaries' tier by the cheapest one that passes an eval.
options.B: Use the top tier for all three tasks, so the whole platform runs on one model family and a single prompt style.
options.C: Use the mid tier for all three tasks and keep revising the dispute prompt until its agreement with counsel reaches 90%.
options.D: Use the mid tier for the classifier and the summaries and the top tier for the disputes, so nothing runs on the smallest tier.

rationale: Each task gets the cheapest tier that clears its own measured bar: the classifier at 2 million a day is where the smallest tier pays off, the 300 monthly disputes have a measured gap that only the top tier closes and a tiny volume, and the summaries have no evidence yet, so an eval decides. One tier everywhere (B) overspends on the high-volume tasks. More revisions on the mid tier (C) already plateaued at 78%. Avoiding the smallest tier (D) pays for capability the classifier was shown not to need.
evidence: Select the least expensive model that meets a measured quality bar per task, using evals, and reserve more capable tiers for tasks that need them.

task: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
question:
A bank's support assistant gives answers of inconsistent length and often skips the escalation step. This is the relevant part of its system prompt.

```text
You are a support assistant for Meridian Bank.
Always keep answers under 50 words.
Explain every fee fully, including how it is calculated and when it can be waived.
Never give financial advice.
If the customer sounds upset, make sure they feel heard and offer recommendations to improve their situation.
Escalate to a human agent when appropriate.
```

What should the architect change first?

options.A: Rewrite the rules so precedence is explicit, advice is defined, and escalation has concrete triggers.
options.B: Move the rules out of the system prompt and into each user message, so they sit closer to the question.
options.C: Tag each rule with a label such as CRITICAL or HIGH, so the model can weight the rules against one another.
options.D: Move the assistant to a larger model, which should resolve the ambiguity more reliably.

rationale: The prompt contradicts itself: 50 words versus a full fee explanation, no advice versus offering recommendations, and escalation with no trigger. Fixing the rules so conflicts have a stated winner and vague terms become concrete removes the cause; the model then no longer has to guess. Labels (C) assign weight without resolving which rule wins in a given case. Moving rules to the user turn (B) does not change their content, and a larger model (D) still has to guess at an underspecified policy.
evidence: Prompts work best when instructions are clear, specific and non-contradictory, with the desired behavior explained rather than left ambiguous.

task: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

options.A: Require the rationale to run at least 200 words, so the model explains how the rules interact in more depth.
options.B: Put a reasoning field before the decision, or let the model think first, so the label follows.
options.C: Remove the rationale field, so the model commits to a label without a justification that it can contradict.
options.D: Add a confidence number after the decision and send low-confidence cases to human reviewers.

rationale: The schema makes the model emit the decision first and the rationale afterward, so the rationale only explains a label already chosen. Having it reason before it commits (a reasoning field first, or thinking enabled) lets the interacting rules be worked through before the label is produced. A longer rationale (A) is still written after the label. Dropping it (C) removes the reasoning that helps. A confidence score (D) routes errors to reviewers without improving the model's accuracy.
evidence: Letting Claude reason before giving its final answer improves performance on complex multi-step tasks; the order of output matters.

task: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
question: A customer-support chat keeps the full transcript of every turn, and conversations can run past 120 turns. Cost and latency per turn rise steadily, and answers get worse late in long chats. Customers often state constraints early ("no weekend delivery", an order number) that must still hold at turn 100. Which context strategy fits best?

options.A: Keep only the last 10 turns verbatim and discard everything older than that, to bound the context size.
options.B: Replace older turns with a running summary that keeps constraints and identifiers; leave recent turns verbatim.
options.C: Store every turn externally and retrieve the 10 earlier turns that are most similar to each new customer message.
options.D: Enable prompt caching on the whole transcript so the repeated early turns are billed at the cached rate on each turn.

rationale: A rolling summary compresses old history while deliberately preserving the facts that must persist, and recent turns stay exact for flow. Dropping all but 10 turns (A) loses the early constraint. Caching (D) makes the same growing context cheaper but does nothing for its size or the late-chat quality drop. Similarity retrieval (C) pulls turns that resemble the new message, and a constraint like "no weekend delivery" rarely resembles a later question.
evidence: Context is a finite resource that must be curated; summarizing long histories while preserving key details keeps long conversations effective.

task: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
question:
A contract-analysis service sends the same 11,000-token system prompt and 14 tool definitions on every request, with cache_control on the final system block. Costs have not dropped. Usage from two consecutive requests and the tool order as sent are below.

```text
req 1: cache_creation_input_tokens=13400  cache_read_input_tokens=0
req 2: cache_creation_input_tokens=13400  cache_read_input_tokens=0
tools req 1: search_clauses, get_party, lookup_statute, ...
tools req 2: get_party, lookup_statute, search_clauses, ...
note: the tool list is built from a Python set() when each worker starts
```

What is the right fix?

options.A: Send the tool definitions in a fixed, deterministic order so the prefix is identical across requests and workers.
options.B: Move the cache_control marker onto the user message so that the cache boundary falls after the varying content.
options.C: Add more guidance to the system prompt so that the cached prefix is longer than the minimum cacheable length.
options.D: Switch the cache lifetime from 5 minutes to 1 hour, so that the written prefix stays available longer between requests.

rationale: Caching is a prefix match in the order tools, system, messages. Both requests wrote the cache and neither read it, and the tool order differs between workers, so the prefix is not byte-identical and every request starts over. A deterministic tool order fixes the invalidator. A longer TTL (D) cannot help when the prefix never matches. Moving the marker to the user message (B) puts it after the varying content and makes matching worse. The prompt is already far above the minimum length (C), as the 13,400 cache-write tokens show.
evidence: Prompt caching matches on an exact prefix in the order tools, system, messages; any change earlier in the prefix invalidates it, and cache_read_input_tokens shows hits.

task: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
question: A consulting firm maintains 14 Claude assistants. All of them paste the same 1,800-token brand-voice and confidentiality section into their system prompts. Separately, 3 of the assistants occasionally produce board-ready slide decks using a 25-step formatting procedure with template files and a validation script, none of which matters to the other eleven tasks. Which TWO changes fit? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Replace the 14 assistants with a single assistant whose system prompt covers every task and style rule.
options.B: Maintain the shared section as one versioned module from which every assistant's prompt is assembled.
options.C: Package the deck procedure, templates and validation script as a Skill that loads only when a deck is requested.
options.D: Paste the 25-step deck procedure into all 14 system prompts so any assistant can build a deck if asked.
options.E: Include the validation script's source in the prompt so the model can write it out and run it when needed.

rationale: There are two different reuse problems. The shared 1,800-token block is identical everywhere, so a single versioned module (B) removes the drift and gives one place to change it. The deck procedure is large, specialized and needed rarely, which fits a Skill (C): only its short description is loaded up front, the full instructions on demand, and the script runs without its source entering context. Pasting the procedure everywhere (D) taxes every request, merging assistants (A) bloats and mixes tasks, and embedding script source (E) spends tokens a Skill's bundled script avoids.
evidence: Skills load progressively (metadata, then instructions, then resources), and bundled scripts run without their code entering context.

task: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
question: A due-diligence tool sends Claude 12 data-room documents (about 140,000 tokens) plus a question such as "Which agreements contain change-of-control clauses?" Answers sometimes miss clauses in the middle documents or blend text from different files. The prompt currently starts with the question and instructions, then concatenates the documents with no separators. Which prompt change helps most?

options.A: Summarize each document in a separate call and send only the twelve summaries together with the question.
options.B: Put the documents first, each in its own tagged block with its source, then the instructions and question, and ask for relevant quotes first.
options.C: Add an instruction to read every document thoroughly and be exhaustive, while keeping the same layout.
options.D: Retrieve the five chunks most similar to the question and send only those, so the prompt stays short.

rationale: For long inputs, documents belong near the top wrapped in clear structure with their metadata, with the question at the end; asking the model to quote the relevant passages first helps it find clauses in the middle of the context and keeps text attributed to the right file. Summaries (A) drop clause wording, five similar chunks (D) miss clauses that don't resemble the question, and an exhortation (C) leaves the unstructured layout that caused the blending.
evidence: Place long documents above the query, wrap each in tags with source metadata, and ask Claude to quote relevant parts first.

task: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
question: A telecom's billing assistant must stay on billing topics, keep an empathetic tone, and never promise bill credits, which only human agents may grant. Testers found that it occasionally writes "I've applied a $20 credit to your account." The product owner wants the next release to be dependable. Which TWO changes fit? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Describe scope and tone in the system prompt, explain why credits are reserved for humans, and say what to offer instead (a handoff).
options.B: Test the revised prompt on 50 sample conversations and treat the rule as enforced if none of them promises a credit.
options.C: Add a footer to every reply stating that the assistant can make mistakes and that credits are not guaranteed.
options.D: Give the assistant no credit-granting tool, and add an output check that flags credit-commitment language for human review.
options.E: Repeat the no-credits rule at the start, middle and end of the system prompt so the model weighs it more heavily.

rationale: A prompt shapes behavior: stating the scope and tone positively, with the reason and a concrete alternative to say (A), reduces the slips. A must-never rule also needs enforcement outside the model: no tool that can grant credits and a check on output that flags commitment language (D) make the failure caught rather than hoped away. Repetition (E) and a clean 50-case sample (B) are probabilistic and cannot show a rare failure is gone. A disclaimer footer (C) does not stop the promise from being made.
evidence: Prompts describe desired behavior and reasons; rules that must hold are enforced with deterministic controls outside the model.

task: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
question: A routing service on Sonnet 5.5 handles 6 million requests a month, each classifying a short email into one of 20 queues. The requests are configured with effort set to xhigh. Per request the metrics show about 450 input tokens and about 2,900 output tokens, most of them thinking. An eval shows 98% accuracy at xhigh. Which change reduces cost the most while protecting quality?

options.A: Set max_tokens to 300 so that the model cannot produce more than a short answer on any request.
options.B: Enable prompt caching on the system prompt so that the repeated instructions are billed at the cached rate.
options.C: Re-run the eval at lower effort levels and adopt the lowest one that keeps accuracy within the agreed bar.
options.D: Stream the responses, since streamed output tokens are billed at a lower rate than buffered ones.

rationale: Output tokens dominate (2,900 versus 450), and most of them are thinking, which effort controls; a simple 20-way email classification may hold its accuracy at a lower setting, and the eval tells you where. Caching (B) discounts only the small input side. A 300-token cap (A) would truncate the thinking and the answer and end with stop_reason max_tokens. Streaming (D) improves perceived latency and does not change what is billed.
evidence: The effort parameter controls how many tokens Claude spends on thinking and responses, trading depth for cost and latency; thinking tokens are billed as output.

task: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
question: A commercial insurer's underwriters spend about three hours per submission re-keying broker emails, application forms and loss-run PDFs into the rating engine. Premiums must come from that engine, because its rates are filed with regulators and every quote must be reproducible. The COO asks whether Claude can "price the risks" to cut turnaround. Which solution should the architect propose?

options.A: Have Claude extract each submission into a validated schema that feeds the rating engine, with flagged fields reviewed
options.B: Have Claude read each submission and compute the premium itself, showing its reasoning for underwriters to audit
options.C: Give an agent browser access to type each submission into the rating engine's screens and then submit each finished quote itself
options.D: Fine-tune a model on past priced submissions so that it predicts the premium directly from the broker documents

rationale: The cost sits in re-keying, not in pricing, and filed, reproducible rates mean the deterministic engine must stay the source of the premium. Claude adds value by turning unstructured submissions into validated structured input, with low-confidence fields sent to an underwriter (A). (B) and (D) move pricing into a model, breaking reproducibility and the filed-rate constraint. (C) still needs the same extraction, then adds a brittle screen-driving agent with authority to submit quotes where a schema handoff suffices.
evidence: Find the simplest solution possible and increase complexity only when needed; many applications are well served by optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and examples.

task: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
question:
A telecom's email-reply assistant has run for six months. Draft acceptance has stayed near 55%, and the team cannot tell which intents or knowledge-base articles lead to rejected drafts. The current design is below.
```text
1. Inbound email -> intent classifier (Haiku 5.5) -> intent label
2. Retrieve top-5 KB articles for that intent
3. Draft reply (Sonnet 5.5) -> support agent edits in the CRM -> send
4. Logged: email ID, final sent text
5. Monthly: product team reviews the CSAT dashboard
```
What should the architect add to the design first?

options.A: Retrieve the top fifteen articles instead of five so the drafting step has more material to draw on for each intent
options.B: Record per draft whether it was sent, edited or discarded, with the intent, article IDs and prompt version behind it
options.C: Move drafting to Opus 5.5 so that more drafts are accepted without edits, then compare acceptance after a month
options.D: Add a model call that critiques each draft against the retrieved articles and revises it before the agent sees it

rationale: The loop is open: the log keeps only the final text, so nothing ties an edited or discarded draft to the intent, articles or prompt version that produced it (B). With that outcome signal the team can find failing intents, fix articles, and turn rejected drafts into eval cases. (C), (D) and (A) are changes made blind; without the signal nobody can tell whether any of them helps or which stage of the pipeline is failing.
evidence: Start an eval suite with 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures; reading production transcripts shows where and why the system fails.

task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
question: A freight forwarder receives about 2,000 carrier exception messages a day. Each falls into one of nine stable categories, and each category already has its own handling procedure. Customs holds and damaged-goods claims need careful legal reasoning, while the 80% that are plain delay notices need only a templated customer update. One general prompt covering all nine categories is mediocre at both ends. Which pattern fits best?

options.A: An autonomous agent given every category's handling tools, deciding for itself which procedure each message needs
options.B: An orchestrator that splits each message into subtasks, sends them to parallel worker calls and merges the results
options.C: A classifier step that routes each message to a category-specific prompt and a matching model tier
options.D: A prompt chain that runs every message through all nine procedures in turn and keeps the output that applies

rationale: Routing fits distinct, stable categories that are better handled separately and can be classified accurately, and it lets the simple delay notices go to a small, fast model while customs and damage claims go to a stronger one (C). (A) gives up the predictability of known procedures although the next step is not open-ended. (B) suits tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted in advance; each message here belongs to one category. (D) multiplies cost and latency by nine.
evidence: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up task; it suits distinct categories handled separately, such as sending easy queries to smaller models.

task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
question: A B2B analytics vendor wants Claude to resolve customers' failing data-import jobs. Causes vary widely (schema drift, file encodings, expired credentials, upstream API changes), and the number of steps needed to find one cannot be predicted. Diagnosis can run against a sandboxed copy of each job, and support engineers insist on approving any change before it touches production. Which design fits?

options.A: A single model call given the job's error log, which returns the likely cause and a fix for the engineer to apply
options.B: Parallel subagents, one per known cause, that each try a fix in production and report which of them succeeded
options.C: A fixed prompt chain with one diagnostic step per known cause, run in order until one of the checks reports a match
options.D: An agent that investigates in the sandboxed copy with diagnostic tools and proposes a fix for an engineer to approve

rationale: Open-ended problems whose steps cannot be predicted are where an agent earns its cost, and the sandbox plus an approval gate keep its errors recoverable (D). (C) covers only causes known in advance and stops at the first match. (A) cannot inspect the data, credentials or upstream responses beyond what the log shows, so it guesses. (B) acts in production without approval and treats causes that interact as independent.
evidence: Agents suit open-ended problems where the required number of steps is hard to predict; they need extensive testing in sandboxed environments with appropriate guardrails.

task: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
question:
A private-equity firm's due-diligence system uses a lead agent that delegates research to subagents and then writes the final report. A reviewer flags the report on target company Northwind. The run log is excerpted below.
```text
lead -> sub_1: "Research Northwind's subsidiaries and their finances"
lead -> sub_2: "Also look into subsidiary financials for Northwind"
lead -> sub_3: "Research Northwind's litigation history"
sub_1 -> lead: Northwind Iberia revenue 41.2M (EUR, FY2025) ...
sub_2 -> lead: Northwind Iberia revenue 44.6M (USD, FY2024) ...
sub_3 -> lead: 3 open cases, 1 settled ...
lead: report lists two Iberia revenue figures; Northwind UK omitted
```
Which change best addresses the root cause?

options.A: Have the lead give each subagent a distinct scope, its sources and a required output format, including currency
options.B: Increase the number of subagents so that each subsidiary and each research topic receives its own dedicated researcher
options.C: Add a final model pass that removes duplicated paragraphs from the report before it reaches the deal team
options.D: Let every subagent read the others' full context so that they can spot overlaps and reconcile their figures

rationale: Overlapping, vague delegations caused duplicated work, figures in different currencies and fiscal years, and a gap where Northwind UK should be; each subagent needs a distinct objective, sources, an output format and clear boundaries (A). (D) removes the context isolation that makes subagents useful and still leaves scope undefined. (C) hides duplicate text but not the conflicting figures or the missing subsidiary. (B) adds agents without fixing how work is divided or reported.
evidence: Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries; vague delegation led subagents to duplicate work.

task: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
question: An engineering team must migrate a monolith's 40 modules from one ORM to another. The modules share entity definitions, and a change to one often forces changes in its callers. To finish faster, a tech lead proposes eight parallel coding subagents, each assigned five modules, with a merge step at the end. The token budget for the project is tight. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: The eight parallel subagents as proposed, plus a merge agent that resolves conflicts between their edits
options.B: One agent migrating modules in dependency order, with subagents used only for read-only exploration
options.C: Three agents doing the full migration independently, keeping the version that passes the most tests
options.D: Forty subagents, one per module, so that each works in a small context focused on a single module

rationale: Multi-agent setups pay off for parallel, loosely coupled work and use many times the tokens of a single agent; tightly coupled edits over shared definitions are a poor fit, so one agent working in dependency order, with subagents only for isolated exploration, matches both the task and the budget (B). (A) and (D) split interdependent edits across agents that cannot coordinate and push conflicts to a merge step. (C) triples the cost of the entire migration.
evidence: Domains with many dependencies between agents, such as most coding tasks, fit multi-agent systems poorly; multi-agent systems use about 15x the tokens of chat.

task: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
question: A manufacturer wants Claude to produce its 60-page annual sustainability report from about 300 source documents (plant energy logs, supplier audits, HR summaries). A single long prompt produced a draft that skipped two mandated sections and quoted emissions figures no reviewer could trace to a source. The auditors require every figure to be traceable and every mandated section to be present. Which TWO decomposition steps address these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Run the single long prompt five times and keep whichever draft covers the most sections of the mandated outline
options.B: Ask the model to rate its own confidence in each paragraph and drop the paragraphs it scores below a set threshold
options.C: First extract each figure from its source into a table with document references, then write prose only from that table
options.D: Send all 300 documents in one large-context request and ask for the complete report with a citation after each claim
options.E: Generate the report section by section from the mandated outline, with a code check that every section is present

rationale: Prompt chaining through an intermediate artifact makes traceability checkable: figures are extracted with references first, and prose draws only from that table (C). Generating section by section from the mandated outline with a programmatic gate makes completeness verifiable instead of hoped for (E). (D) repeats the failed single pass at a larger scale. (B) relies on self-assessed confidence, which says nothing about provenance. (A) chooses among drafts that carry the same untraceable figures.
evidence: Prompt chaining breaks a task into a sequence of steps, and programmatic checks (gates) on intermediate steps keep the process on track.

task: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
question: An online marketplace screens each new listing for four independent problems: prohibited items, counterfeit brand use, misleading price claims, and contact details that bypass the platform. One combined prompt often catches one problem and misses the others when a listing has several. Policy requires all four checks on every listing, and screening must finish within three seconds of submission. Which design fits best?

options.A: Run four focused checks in parallel, one per problem, and combine their verdicts in code
options.B: Run the combined prompt three times in parallel and flag a listing only when a majority of the runs agree
options.C: Let an agent read each listing and decide which of the four checks are worth running on that listing
options.D: Run the four checks as a prompt chain, each step passing its findings on to the next check in the sequence

rationale: The checks are independent and the combined prompt splits attention, so sectioning them into focused parallel calls improves recall while keeping latency close to a single call (A). (D) gives the same focus but adds up four latencies, which threatens the three-second budget. (B) votes on the same flawed prompt, which tends to repeat the miss. (C) lets the model skip checks that policy requires on every listing.
evidence: Sectioning runs independent subtasks in parallel; with several considerations, LLMs do better when each one is handled by a separate, focused call.

task: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
question:
A retailer's proposed design sends every Claude request synchronously to Opus 5.5. The architect reviews it against the business requirements below.
```text
Use case              Volume/day  Requirement                 Value driver
Store chat answers      40,000    p95 full reply < 4 s        deflection
Catalog attribute fill  25,000    done within 48 h of upload  cost per SKU
Fraud memo drafts          300    within 2 h, analyst signs   analyst time
Measured on Opus 5.5: store chat p95 full reply = 6.2 s;
fraud memo quality rated excellent by analysts
```
Which TWO changes best align the design with these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Turn on streaming for store chat, so that the measured p95 full-reply time falls below the four-second target
options.B: Evaluate a faster tier for store chat against the deflection eval, and switch if quality holds under 4 s p95
options.C: Run catalog attribute fill through the Message Batches API, since its deadline is far longer than batch turnaround
options.D: Move fraud memo drafting to Haiku 5.5, since its volume is the smallest and the switch adds no quality risk
options.E: Submit the fraud memo drafts through the Message Batches API, since analysts can wait for the results

rationale: Catalog fill is asynchronous with a 48-hour window, so the Batches API's lower price and up-to-24-hour processing match its cost driver (C). Store chat misses its full-reply target on Opus, so a faster tier is the lever, adopted only if the deflection eval holds (B). (E) risks the two-hour memo window, because a batch may take up to 24 hours. (D) chases negligible savings on 300 memos and risks the quality analysts rate excellent. (A) shortens time to first token, not the full-reply time the requirement measures.
evidence: The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at a 50% discount; most batches finish within an hour, with results available within 24 hours.

task: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
question: A hospital network wants to cut the two hours of after-hours charting its primary-care physicians do each day. A vendor demo shows an agent that writes visit notes and files them straight into the EHR. Hospital policy requires the treating physician to review and sign every note, and notes must be complete before the end of the clinic day. Which solution best serves the stated goal?

options.A: A draft note generated from each visit's transcript, placed in the EHR for the physician to edit and sign
options.B: An agent that writes visit notes and files them into the EHR, with a weekly audit of a sample of the filed notes
options.C: An assistant that answers physicians' questions about documentation rules while they write each note by hand
options.D: A nightly batch job that summarizes each day's visits so that physicians can review all notes the next morning

rationale: The value pillar is physician time under a mandatory sign-off, so Claude should produce a draft from each visit that the physician edits and signs during the day, with time-to-sign as the measure (A). (B) bypasses the required review. (D) misses the same-day completeness rule and shifts the work to the next morning instead of removing it. (C) helps with rules but leaves the writing, which is where the time goes.
evidence: Start with the simplest design that meets the need; augmented LLM calls can include human checkpoints where review is required.

task: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
question: Associates at a law firm use a Claude research assistant over the firm's knowledge base. When an answer is wrong they email the practice-support team, which edits the prompt by hand; last month one such edit silently broke answers about limitation periods. The managing partner wants two things: corrections captured in a form that shows what produced each bad answer, and confidence that a fix does not break what already works. Which TWO additions meet these needs? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Fine-tune a model every night on that day's corrections, so the same mistakes stop recurring the next day
options.B: An in-app flag with a short correction, saved with the trace ID that links it to the passages and prompt version
options.C: Raise the number of retrieved passages automatically whenever the weekly count of flagged answers goes up
options.D: Append each associate's emailed correction to the system prompt as a new rule, so the assistant learns from it
options.E: Confirmed failures added to a regression eval suite that every prompt or retrieval change must pass to ship

rationale: Capturing flags in the product, tied to the trace, links each bad answer to the passages and prompt version behind it (B). Turning confirmed failures into a regression suite that gates every change prevents the silent breakage seen last month (E). (D) grows the prompt with unreviewed, possibly conflicting rules through the same manual process that caused the regression. (A) trains on unvetted labels with no regression check. (C) changes retrieval on a volume signal without diagnosing a cause.
evidence: Regression evals check that the system still handles what it used to and should pass at nearly 100%, protecting against backsliding.

task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
question: A cosmetics brand localizes product copy into 12 languages. Native reviewers apply clear written criteria: a 140-term brand glossary that must be used exactly, and tone rules for each market. First drafts often break the glossary, and reviewers find that pointing out the violations and asking for a revision fixes most of them. New copy is published once a week. Which pattern fits best?

options.A: An orchestrator that decides at run time which languages each product needs and delegates them to workers
options.B: A generator paired with an evaluator that checks each draft against the glossary and tone rules, with a revision cap
options.C: A router that classifies each product by category and sends it to a category-specific translation prompt
options.D: An autonomous agent with web search that studies each market's competitor copy before it writes its own localized text

rationale: Evaluator-optimizer fits when evaluation criteria are clear and iterative feedback measurably improves the output, which is what the reviewers observed (B); the glossary part can even be checked in code. (C) addresses differences between product categories, not glossary violations. (A) solves a planning problem that does not exist, since the target languages are fixed. (D) adds cost and unpredictability without enforcing the glossary.
evidence: Evaluator-optimizer: one LLM generates and another evaluates and gives feedback in a loop; it works when criteria are clear and iteration adds measurable value.

task: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
question: An auto insurer's Claude classifier flags first-notice-of-loss reports that mention bodily injury, so that an adjuster calls within one hour. About 3% of reports involve injury. Missing one exposes the insurer to regulatory penalties, while a false flag costs a few minutes of adjuster time. The vendor reports 96% accuracy on a random sample of 1,000 reports. Which primary metric should the architect require?

options.A: Macro-averaged F1 across all claim categories, so every category counts equally in one combined score
options.B: Recall on injury reports, measured on enough injury cases to be reliable, with a floor on precision
options.C: An LLM-judge score of how well the classifier explains each flag, graded against a written rubric
options.D: Overall accuracy on a larger random sample, so that the 96% figure carries a tighter confidence interval

rationale: With a 3% positive rate, a classifier that never flags injury scores about 97% accuracy, so accuracy says nothing about the costly error. Recall on the injury class, measured on an adequate number of injury cases, with a precision floor to cap wasted calls, matches the asymmetric costs (B). (D) refines the wrong number. (A) blends the critical class with categories whose errors cost little. (C) grades explanations, not whether injuries are caught.
evidence: Good success criteria are specific and measurable and reflect the use case, using task-fidelity measures such as F1 or recall where they fit.

task: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
question: A company is launching an IT helpdesk agent that can reset passwords and change group memberships through directory tools.
